Cinema’s Temporal Gaze

Cinema’s Temporal Gaze

Every film is made in one year and set in another — and most of the time those are the same year. Pick a decade and watch where its films look: back below the line, forward above it, and the great still mass of films set in their own present collapsed into the grey bar at the centre.

—

Checked against 662 films labelled independently by hand, the classifier puts a film in the right category 90% of the time and lands the depicted year within 2 years 90% of the time. That splits: 95% where the summary actually names a year, 85% where the model is going on what it knows about the film.

Looks back (set before release) Looks ahead (set after release) Set in its own present Thicker lines carry more of their film’s attention

What each decade did with its time

A median tells you the middle film and nothing about the spread, so here is the spread. One bar per release decade, counting only the films that actually travel: everything set in its own present is pulled out and reported on the right, because at 60 to 80% of every decade it would flatten everything else into a sliver. Reading left to right you are walking from the deep past, through the near past, across the line, and out into the future; the darker the shade, the further that slice goes. Decades with fewer than ten films to count are left out rather than guessed at.

Every film at once

The year a film came out along the bottom, the year it depicts up the side, one dot for every year any film points at. The diagonal is cinema set in its own moment, and almost everything sits on it. Below that line is memory; above it is speculation — and you can see at a glance how much thinner the air gets up there. The decade you picked above is drawn solid, the rest faint behind it. This is also the sanity check: if this and the arcs disagree, the aggregation is wrong.

What falls out of the data

Look up a film

Type a title and see what this project decided about it: the year it came out, the year it depicts, and the gap between them. Original titles work too, in their own script — Le Voyage dans la Lune finds A Trip to the Moon, and 千と千尋の神隠し finds Spirited Away. Search reads the whole labelled corpus, not just the decade selected above, but it does respect the genre and origin filters.

How this was built, and what is wrong with it
  • Corpus. 6187 films from TMDB, 1900–2026, sampled per release year and ranked within the year by TMDB vote count, covering 51 national cinemas across 10 regions. It is not evenly spread: the United States alone is 38% of it, so any figure you read without picking an origin is mostly a statement about American cinema. Vote count is a popularity measure, and popularity travels badly between film industries — a well-known film from a small country can sit below an obscure one from a large one.
  • Labels are model judgments, not extractions. 49% of films were classified from world knowledge rather than from a stated year in the source text, because the source text is a ~90-word summary that usually does not name the setting.
  • The labels have now been scored. Against 662 films labelled by hand through a different process, the model agrees on gaze 90% of the time and on the depicted year (within 2y) 90% of the time. The split by basis is the interesting part: 95% where the source text states a year against 85% where it does not, so the cheap model is meaningfully worse — but not guessing — when the text is silent. This is agreement between two labelsets, not truth: both could be wrong the same way, and the hand set is itself a judgment call on the hard cases.
  • Present is the default and the default is sticky. A film whose setting is never stated and that the model does not recognise lands on "present". That biases the whole picture toward the diagonal, so real nostalgia is probably understated.
  • Medians, never means. One film set in the year 802,701 outweighs a thousand set last Tuesday. Every figure here is a median; the means are meaningless and are not shown.
  • The year axis is piecewise. The dense 1850–2050 band gets most of the width; deep past and far future are compressed, with dashed breaks marking the joins. Distances across a break are not comparable.
  • Re-releases contaminate. A 2013 3-D re-release of a 1993 film reads as a 20-year lookback. Rare, but present.

Film metadata — titles, release years, countries, genres and summaries — comes from TMDB. It does not vet, endorse or certify anything on this page; the classifications, the aggregation and every claim made from them are this project's own.
